short: The king who ruled without Parliament, lost a civil war, and was executed.
full:
Charles I inherited his father's belief in the divine right of kings and none of his flexibility. Disputes over taxation, the forced loan and the Petition of Right led him to dissolve Parliament in 1629 and govern for eleven years without one, financing the state through ship money and other prerogative levies. Archbishop Laud's ceremonial reforms alienated Puritans, and imposing a new prayer book on Scotland in 1637 provoked a war that forced Charles to recall Parliament in 1640.

The Long Parliament dismantled the machinery of personal rule and then split with the king over control of the army after the Irish rebellion. Fighting began in August 1642. Defeats at Marston Moor and Naseby left Charles a prisoner by 1646, and his negotiations with the Scots restarted the war in 1648, destroying what trust remained. He was tried by a specially constituted High Court and beheaded outside the Banqueting House at Whitehall on 30 January 1649.
